documents.title: Drafting a generative AI-use policy for your course
documents.summary: A teaching-center guide telling instructors to write a clear AI policy in their syllabus, with a checklist of components, advice on tone and revision, and four sample policies ranging from near-ban to required AI use. It also gives conditions on AI detectors and a list of strategies to reduce unauthorized AI use.
documents.stance_why: The guide sets no campus-wide rule on student AI use; it says "we recommend that you design an generative AI policy that aligns with the specific ethics and practices of your discipline, your department, and your course" and offers four sample policies to adapt, so the decision rests with instructors.

units.why: The guide says "it’s important that you include a clear AI-use policy in your syllabus", addressed to instructors, so it requires a syllabus statement (P09), not a stance.
units.anchor: it’s important that you include a clear AI-use policy in your syllabus

units.why: The sentence "your students won’t know what is expected, what is allowed, and what is prohibited" gives the reason for stating a policy. I chose P09 because it supports the syllabus-statement duty; P66 is about discussing reasons with students, which it does not say.
units.anchor: your students won’t know what is expected, what is allowed, and what is prohibited
units.fit_note: States the consequence of omitting a syllabus policy rather than the duty itself.

units.why: "Students desire clarity from you" cites a survey (Flaherty, 2025) as evidence about what students want; coded P55 (evidence cited), though it is not about learning outcomes.
units.anchor: Students desire clarity from you on the ethical and allowable uses
units.fit_note: Cites survey evidence about student preferences for clarity, not evidence on learning or performance.

units.why: "We recommend that you design an generative AI policy that aligns with the specific ethics and practices of your discipline, your department, and your course" recommends tailoring policy to context; the decision rests with each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: aligns with the specific ethics and practices of your discipline, your department, and your course

units.why: "edit it in accordance with your expectations for your course" tells instructors to adapt the sample language, leaving wording and stance to each course (P04).

units.why: "AI detection tools are neither accurate nor reliable" cites Weber-Wulff et al. and says detectors are unreliable, matching P39.

units.why: "If they are used, they should be used with caution" allows detectors but advises care; it fits P39 only partly because detectors are not ruled out. I chose P39 over P40 since the emphasis is caution about unreliability.

units.frag_start: If they are used, they should
units.fit_note: Permits detector use but with caution, rather than refusing to rely on detectors.

units.why: "at UC Santa Cruz, there are specific conditions that must be met" for detection software (local hosting, campus contract, or written student approval) is an approval and data-protection condition on a tool, so P65 (review and approval of AI tools, data sharing) fits best.
units.anchor: there are specific conditions that must be met: the detection software is hosted locally
units.policy: At UC Santa Cruz, AI detection software may be used only if it is hosted locally and data is protected from external access, contracted through campus purchasing, or prior written approval is obtained from all students.

units.why: "Let your learning outcomes be your guide" says any choice to prevent, allow or require AI should support learning outcomes, which is P83.
